fieldData.short-description: A form is where a visitor becomes a lead, which makes it one of the most important things on your site. What Webflow’s native forms do well, where they fall short, and how to turn them into a lead engine.
fieldData.tl-dr: A form is where a visitor becomes a lead, so it’s one of the most important things on your site, not a technical afterthought. Webflow’s native forms are clean, easy, and enough for most marketing forms, and they connect directly to tools like HubSpot, Zapier, and Make. They hit limits when you need conditional logic, multi-step flows, or stronger spam protection, which is where a third-party form tool earns its place. This guide covers what native forms do well, where they fall short, how to connect them to your CRM, the spam and GDPR issues that trip teams up, and how to design forms that actually convert. The short version: start native, add a third-party tool only when a real need shows up, and never lose sight of where the lead goes after submit.
fieldData.content:
Forms are where leads actually convert

On most marketing sites, the form is the moment everything else has been working toward. All the traffic, the content, the design, the positioning, it all leads to someone deciding to fill in their details and hit submit. That makes the form one of the highest-stakes elements on your entire site, even though it’s often treated as a minor technical detail bolted on at the end.

For a marketing team, that reframing matters. A form isn’t just a way to collect an email. It’s the conversion point of your whole funnel, and small things about it, how long it is, whether it works on mobile, whether the submission actually reaches your CRM, directly affect how many leads you capture and keep. A beautiful site with a broken or badly designed form is leaking pipeline every day.

So this guide treats Webflow forms the way a marketing team should: not as “how to drag a form block onto a page,” but as how to make forms that reliably capture leads and feed them into the systems where your team works. We’ll cover what Webflow gives you out of the box, where you’ll outgrow it, and how to get the whole chain, from submit to CRM, working properly.

Native forms: strengths and limits

What Webflow’s built-in forms handle well, and where they run out of road.

What Webflow’s native forms do well

Webflow has form functionality built in, and for a lot of marketing needs it’s genuinely all you need. It’s worth being clear about its real strengths before talking about limits.

The biggest advantage is that native forms are fully integrated with your site’s design. You build and style the form with Webflow’s own design tools, so it matches your brand exactly, with no embedding, no iframe, no styling conflicts. Forms built natively render cleanly, stay responsive on mobile, and don’t carry the visual mismatches that embedded third-party forms often introduce. For a team that cares how the site looks, that seamlessness is a real benefit.

They’re also simple to set up and manage. You drag a form onto the page, customize the fields, set the success and error messages, and choose who gets notified, all without code. Submissions can be collected in Webflow itself and viewed in your site settings, and paid plans support unlimited submissions. For a standard contact form, demo request, or newsletter signup, that’s often everything required.

And they connect directly to the tools you already use. Native Webflow forms can send submissions straight to apps like HubSpot, Zapier, and Make, which means a form can feed your CRM or trigger an automation without a third-party form service in between. For most marketing forms, native is the simplest place to start, and the simplest setup is usually the one that keeps working.

Where native forms hit limits

Native forms are a great starting point, but they have real limits, and knowing them up front saves you from discovering them mid-campaign.

The most common one is conditional logic. Webflow’s native forms don’t support showing or hiding fields based on previous answers, so if you need a form that adapts as someone fills it in, native alone won’t do it. The same goes for multi-step forms, breaking a longer form into stages, which native doesn’t handle on its own and which often needs a third-party tool or custom work.

Then there’s spam and notifications. Webflow’s form endpoint is predictable, which means bots can sometimes bypass the standard frontend reCAPTCHA by posting directly to it, a real issue for teams running paid traffic to a landing page. Email notifications, while usually fine, are occasionally unreliable, and the native interface for viewing and managing submissions is fairly basic, with no easy way to edit entries. None of these is a dealbreaker for a simple form, but they add up if forms are central to your lead generation.

Finally, there are plan limits to be aware of. Form submission limits and certain features depend on your Webflow plan, so a high-volume site needs to check that its plan matches its actual submission volume. The honest summary is that native forms are excellent for standard use and start to strain when your needs get more advanced, which is exactly when a third-party tool becomes worth considering.

Native vs third-party: how to choose

The practical question most teams face is when to stick with native forms and when to bring in a dedicated form tool. Here’s a clear way to decide.

Use native Webflow forms when you want a clean, lightweight setup that matches your design, your forms are relatively standard (contact, demo request, newsletter, basic lead capture), and you’re happy connecting to your CRM through Webflow’s built-in app integrations. For most marketing sites, this covers the majority of forms, and it’s the simplest, most maintainable option.

Reach for a third-party form tool when you need something native can’t do: conditional logic, multi-step flows, advanced spam protection, built-in A/B testing, or tighter, more configurable CRM and automation workflows. Tools in this space include options like HubSpot Forms (strong if you’re already in HubSpot), lightweight services like Formspark, and Webflow-native form apps like Inputflow for multi-step flows built inside the Designer, among others. Each is suited to different priorities, so the right one depends on what specifically you need that native lacks.

One important technical note when choosing a third-party tool: how it integrates with Webflow matters a lot. Tools that embed via iframe often cause styling conflicts, break on mobile, or lose tracking data, while tools that render natively (as a web component or a true Webflow app) keep your design and tracking intact. If you do go third-party, favor one that integrates cleanly rather than one bolted on through an iframe.

Use native Webflow forms if... Reach for a third-party tool if...
Your forms are standard (contact, demo, newsletter) You need conditional logic (fields that adapt)
You want a clean, on-brand, lightweight setup You need multi-step forms broken into stages
You connect to your CRM via HubSpot, Zapier, or Make You need stronger, layered spam protection
You want the simplest thing to manage You want built-in A/B testing on forms
You're happy with Webflow's built-in submissions You need tighter, more configurable CRM workflows

Connecting forms to your CRM and tools

Capturing a submission is only half the job. Where the lead goes next is what actually matters for a marketing team, and this is the part worth getting right.

A form submission should rarely just sit in your site settings. For it to be useful, it needs to reach the place your team works: your CRM, your email platform, your task system, or an automation that routes it appropriately. Webflow’s native forms can connect directly to HubSpot, Zapier, and Make, which between them can route a submission almost anywhere. A HubSpot connection syncs leads straight into your CRM. A Zapier or Make connection can send the data to hundreds of other tools, notify a Slack channel, create a task, or kick off a multi-step workflow.

For teams with more complex routing, webhooks are the underlying mechanism worth knowing about. A webhook fires when a form is submitted and sends the data wherever you point it, which is how you connect forms to custom workflows, route different submissions to different places, or trigger automations beyond simple email notifications. If your setup relies on webhooks or region-based routing (sending leads to different workflows depending on where they’re from, for example), the important thing is to test both the data mapping and the downstream workflow properly, because a silently broken connection means lost leads.

The principle for a marketing team is simple: design the whole chain, not just the form. From the field a visitor fills in, to the CRM record, to the follow-up that gets triggered, the entire path should be intentional and tested. That’s the difference between a form that collects emails and a form that actually drives pipeline.

Spam, GDPR, and the things that break

A few practical issues catch teams off guard with forms, and they’re worth handling deliberately rather than discovering the hard way.

Spam is the first. Because Webflow’s form endpoint is predictable, bots can bypass standard frontend reCAPTCHA by posting directly to it, which is especially a problem for landing pages running paid traffic. Effective protection usually means more than the default reCAPTCHA: layered measures like honeypot fields, server-side filtering, or stronger validation through a third-party tool. If you’re seeing spam submissions pile up, the default protection isn’t enough on its own.

GDPR is the second, and it matters especially for teams with EU traffic, which includes most of Europe. One specific catch: Google reCAPTCHA automatically loads Google Fonts and makes requests to Google’s servers, which can transfer user data outside the EU without explicit consent, a genuine GDPR concern. If you target EU users, this is worth checking with whoever handles your compliance, and considering a privacy-first alternative. More broadly, any form collecting personal data from EU residents needs proper consent, clear data handling, and a data processing agreement with any third-party form processor you use.

The third is the quiet one: broken connections. Email notifications can occasionally fail, and integrations can silently stop working, which means leads vanish without anyone noticing. The fix is process, not technology: test your forms regularly, confirm submissions are actually arriving where they should, and check the whole chain after any change to your site or integrations. A form you haven’t tested in three months is a form you can’t trust.

Form design that converts

Beyond the technical side, how a form is designed has a direct effect on how many people complete it. This is where marketing instinct matters as much as setup.

The most reliable rule is to ask for as little as possible. Every additional field reduces completion, so a form should request only what you genuinely need at that stage. A newsletter signup needs an email, not a phone number and company size. A demo request needs enough to follow up, not a full profile. If you don’t need a field to take the next step, cutting it will usually lift your conversion rate more than any clever tactic.

Clarity and trust do the rest. A form should have a clear, specific button (“Get the guide” or “Book a demo” beats a generic “Submit”), a visible reason to fill it in, and a clean layout that doesn’t feel like a wall of fields. It has to work flawlessly on mobile, where a large share of visitors will encounter it, and it should show a clear success message so people know it worked. For longer forms that you genuinely can’t shorten, breaking them into steps can reduce the intimidation of a single long page, which is one of the cases where a multi-step third-party tool earns its place.

The throughline is that good form design and good marketing are the same thing: respect the visitor’s time, make the value obvious, and remove every bit of friction between interest and submission.

What to actually do

Pulling it together, here’s the practical approach to Webflow forms for a marketing team.

Start native. For most forms, Webflow’s built-in forms are clean, on-brand, simple to manage, and connect directly to your CRM through HubSpot, Zapier, or Make. They’ll handle the majority of what a marketing site needs, and the simplest setup is the one most likely to keep working. Add a third-party tool only when a real need shows up, conditional logic, multi-step flows, stronger spam protection, or A/B testing, and when you do, choose one that integrates cleanly rather than through an iframe.

Then take care of the things that quietly cost you leads. Handle spam with more than the default protection if you run paid traffic, check your GDPR position if you have EU visitors, and test the whole chain from submit to CRM regularly so nothing fails silently. And design every form around conversion: ask for as little as possible, make the value clear, and make it flawless on mobile. Get this right and your forms stop being a technical detail and start being one of the most productive parts of your marketing.

fieldData.short-description: Webflow gives marketing teams a real edge for lead generation, if you set it up the right way. How to turn it into a pipeline engine with fast pages, gated content, and forms that convert.
fieldData.tl-dr: Webflow gives B2B marketing teams a real advantage for lead generation: fast pages, the freedom to ship and test without a developer, a CMS that scales landing pages and gated content, and native connections to your CRM. But the platform is the foundation, not the strategy. This guide covers how to actually use Webflow for lead gen: the speed and autonomy advantage, landing pages at scale, gated content libraries, forms that convert, CRM integration, and how to measure what works. The honest throughline is that Webflow makes good lead gen easier to execute, but execution is still on you.
fieldData.content:
Why the platform matters for lead generation

Every B2B marketing team wants the same thing from its website: more qualified leads, captured reliably, handed cleanly to sales. The question is how much the platform you build on actually helps you get there.

The answer is: more than people think, but not in the way most articles claim. You’ll read a lot of posts that treat Webflow as a lead generation machine, as if switching platforms is what generates pipeline. That’s not quite right. Webflow doesn’t generate leads. Your strategy does. What Webflow does is remove the friction that slows good strategy down, so the team executing it can move faster, test more, and ship without waiting on engineering.

That distinction matters, because it sets the right expectation. If your positioning is weak, your offers are generic, and your content doesn’t speak to a real buyer, no platform will fix that. But if you have a real strategy and the right platform, the platform becomes a genuine advantage. This guide is about making Webflow that advantage. Everything below assumes you’ve done the strategic work, and focuses on how Webflow helps you execute it well.

The Webflow advantage: speed and autonomy

Two things make Webflow genuinely good for B2B lead generation, and they compound each other. The first is speed, in the literal sense. Webflow sites load fast by default, with high PageSpeed scores out of the box and global delivery through a CDN. For B2B lead gen, this matters more than it sounds. A meaningful share of prospects research on mobile, often between meetings, and a slow page loses them before they see your offer. Fast pages keep more of the traffic you worked to earn, which means more of it reaches your forms.

The second is autonomy, and this is the bigger one. Webflow lets marketing teams build, edit, and ship without a developer in the loop for routine work. A new campaign landing page doesn’t wait in an engineering queue. A copy test on a hero doesn’t need a deploy. A new gated asset goes live the same day someone finishes it. For lead generation, where success comes from testing and iterating quickly, that independence is the whole game. The team that can ship ten landing page variations in the time another team ships two will learn faster and generate more pipeline, with the same headcount.

Speed and autonomy together mean a marketing team can run lead gen at its own pace, not at the pace of whoever controls the codebase. That’s the core of why Webflow works for this.

Building blocks

What you actually build to turn a Webflow site into a lead engine.

Landing pages at scale

Lead generation runs on landing pages: campaign pages, offer pages, webinar pages, partner pages, comparison pages. The more targeted each one is, the better it converts. The problem on most platforms is that producing them is slow, so teams reuse a generic page instead of building a focused one.

Webflow changes the math two ways. First, you can build a strong landing page template once and clone it for each new campaign, swapping copy and imagery in minutes rather than rebuilding from scratch. Second, for programmatic plays, the Webflow CMS can generate large numbers of structured landing pages from a single data source: one template, hundreds of pages, each targeting a specific keyword, industry, or use case. For a B2B team chasing long-tail search demand, that’s a way to capture intent at scale without hand-building every page.

The practical effect is that targeted landing pages stop being a luxury you ration and become something you produce as fast as campaigns demand. That alone tends to lift conversion, because a prospect who lands on a page built for their exact situation converts better than one who lands on a generic homepage.

Gated content and resource libraries

Gated content (whitepapers, reports, templates, tools) is a core B2B lead gen motion, and it’s an area where Webflow’s CMS does real work.

Instead of building each gated asset as a one-off page, you build a resource template once and let the CMS handle the rest. Each new whitepaper or report becomes a CMS item that generates its own landing page, its own gated form, and its own entry in a filterable resource library. As the library grows, visitors can search and filter it (with a tool like Jetboost), which keeps older assets discoverable instead of buried.

The strategic advantage is that scaling your gated content stops being an engineering cost. A marketing team can add a new gated asset whenever they produce one, without a developer building a new page each time. Over a year, that’s the difference between a resource library with five assets and one with fifty, and the larger library captures far more leads across far more topics.

A note on balance: gating everything is a mistake, because it suppresses the SEO and AEO value of your best content. The common approach is to keep genuinely useful content ungated for visibility, and reserve gating for high-value assets where a prospect will trade their details for real depth. Webflow makes both easy; the judgment about what to gate is the strategic part.

Forms and lead capture that convert

The form is where a visitor becomes a lead, so it deserves more thought than it usually gets. Webflow’s native forms handle the fundamentals well: they’re easy to build, style to match your brand, and connect to your stack. For most lead capture, they’re all you need. The main principle that improves conversion is asking for less. Every additional field costs you completions. The common practice is to capture the minimum that lets sales act (often a work email, a name, and a company) and enrich the rest later from data tools rather than making the prospect type it all.

For more involved capture (multi-step qualification, surveys, a product-fit quiz) a conversational tool like Typeform often converts better than a long static form, because answering one question at a time feels lighter than facing a wall of fields. The rule of thumb: use Webflow’s native forms for straightforward capture, and reach for a specialized tool when the form itself is part of the experience.

Whatever you use, two things matter. The lead has to arrive in your CRM reliably and immediately, and the prospect should get a clear, fast response. A lead that sits unrouted for a day is often a lead lost, which is why the connection to your stack is as important as the form itself.

Connecting to your CRM and marketing stack

A captured lead that doesn’t reach your CRM cleanly is wasted, so the integration layer is not optional. This is where lead gen either works as a system or breaks into manual steps.

Webflow connects to the B2B marketing stack in a few ways. HubSpot integrates closely, so form submissions can flow straight into the CRM as contacts, ready for scoring and nurture sequences. For other tools, Zapier and Make connect Webflow to thousands of services, so a single form submission can create a CRM record, notify sales in Slack, add the lead to a nurture sequence, and log it in a spreadsheet, all automatically.

The goal is a path with no manual steps between a prospect submitting a form and sales being able to act on it. When that path is automated, leads get followed up while they’re still warm. When it isn’t, leads fall through the gaps between tools. The integration work is unglamorous, but it’s often the difference between a lead gen motion that compounds and one that leaks.

Measuring what works

You can’t improve lead gen you can’t see, so measurement closes the loop. The aim is to know which pages, offers, and sources actually produce qualified leads, not just traffic. A practical B2B measurement setup on Webflow combines a few layers: standard analytics for traffic and source data, Webflow-aware analytics like Nocodelytics for CMS and interaction data that standard tools miss, and session tools like Microsoft Clarity to watch how prospects actually move through key pages. Together these answer the questions that matter: which landing pages convert, which gated assets pull the most leads, where prospects drop off in a form, and which traffic sources send people who actually become pipeline.

The point of measuring isn’t the dashboard. It’s the next decision. Good measurement tells you which page to double down on, which offer to retire, and which form field is costing you completions, so each cycle of testing is informed rather than guessed.

The honest part: platform and strategy together

Here’s the throughline. Webflow is a genuinely strong platform for B2B lead generation. The speed keeps your traffic, the autonomy lets you test fast, the CMS scales your pages and gated content, and the integrations connect it all to your pipeline. These are real advantages, and a team that uses them well has a meaningful edge over a team fighting a slow, developer-gated site.

But the platform is the foundation, not the strategy. Webflow makes good lead gen far easier to execute, and it removes the friction that kills momentum. What it can’t do is decide who your buyer is, what offer will move them, or what story makes them trust you. That part is still the work of the marketing team, and it’s still where most of the outcome is decided.

The teams that win at B2B lead gen treat the two as partners. They get the strategy right (clear positioning, real offers, content that speaks to a buyer), and then they use Webflow to execute it faster and test it harder than their competitors can. Get both right, and the website stops being a brochure and starts being one of the most productive parts of the funnel.

fieldData.meta-title: How to delete a CMS collection page in Webflow | Nues
fieldData.meta-description: How to delete a Webflow CMS collection page without breaking your site or SEO: back up, remove connections, set redirects, and when to unpublish instead.
fieldData.short-description: Deleting a CMS collection page is simple to do and easy to get wrong. How to do it safely, without breaking links, losing content, or quietly damaging your SEO.
fieldData.tl-dr: Deleting a CMS collection page in Webflow is simple to do and easy to get wrong, since it can break links, dynamic content, and your SEO. The safe way: back up first, because deletion can't be undone, then delete the collection items, remove every connection, and delete the collection itself. Set up 301 redirects for the old URLs to protect your SEO, consider unpublishing if you might need the content later, and test everything afterward.
fieldData.content:
Deleting a collection page isn’t just a design action

A CMS collection page in Webflow is a dynamic template that automatically generates a page for every item in a collection, every blog post, case study, or product, for example. Because these pages often power content that ranks in search and links throughout your site, deleting one is a structural change, not just a bit of tidying up. Done carelessly, it can leave broken links, empty sections, and lost search rankings. Done properly, it’s straightforward and safe. This guide walks through the safe way, based on Webflow’s own process.

Before you delete: back up first

This is the step people skip and regret. Deleting a collection cannot be undone, unless you restore from a backup. So before you touch anything, save a manual backup of your site by pressing Command + Shift + S on Mac, or Control + Shift + S on Windows. It takes a second and it’s your safety net if something goes wrong. If the collection pages hold content you might want later, it’s also worth exporting the content first.

How to delete the collection page, step by step

Webflow won’t let you delete a collection while things are still connected to it, which is a safeguard against losing data that’s used elsewhere. So the process goes in order:

  1. Back up your site (see above).
  2. Delete the collection items. In the CMS panel, open the collection, select all items (bulk-edit), and delete them. Wait for the site to save.
  3. Remove all connections. In the collection’s settings, click “View Connections” to see every page, template, and symbol tied to the collection. Disconnect each instance, Webflow lets you do this in one click per connection.
  4. Delete the collection. Once every item and connection is gone, go to the CMS panel, open the collection settings, and click Delete. This also removes the collection page.

One thing worth knowing: deleting the collection page template alone doesn’t delete the collection itself. If you want the whole thing gone, you delete the collection (which removes the page). If you only want to remove specific pages, that’s a different situation, and often unpublishing is the better move (more on that below).

The step people forget: set up redirects

This is the most important step for anyone who cares about SEO, and the one most tutorials rush past. If the collection pages you’re deleting rank in Google or are linked to from elsewhere, deleting them without redirects means anyone who visits those URLs hits a broken page, and you lose the search equity those pages built. The fix is to set up 301 redirects that point the old URLs to a sensible new destination (a related page, or the relevant section of your site). Properly implemented redirects preserve the large majority of that link equity. In Webflow, you add redirects in your site settings, and for a whole collection you can often set one redirect rule rather than one per item. If you take one thing from this guide, make it this: never delete ranking pages without redirects.

When to unpublish instead of delete

Deletion is permanent, and it isn’t always the right call. If you’re restructuring your site, pausing content, or think you might need the collection again, there are gentler options that keep your structure intact. You can unpublish collection pages to hide them temporarily without deleting anything, which is ideal when you’re mid-redesign or reworking your content. You can also keep the collection but stop linking to it, if the issue is visibility rather than the data itself. The rule of thumb: if you’re certain you’ll never need it again, delete it properly with redirects. If there’s any doubt, unpublish instead, it’s reversible, and it costs you nothing.

Test your site after deleting

Deletion can have knock-on effects, so always check your site afterward rather than assuming it worked cleanly. Test the old URLs in an incognito window to confirm your redirects resolve properly instead of landing on broken pages. Walk the pages that used to display the collection to make sure no layouts broke or sections are sitting empty. And if the collection was tied to any forms, automations, or integrations, verify those still work. A few minutes of checking catches problems before your visitors, or Google, do.

Quick recap

Deleting a CMS collection page in Webflow is safe when you do it in order: back up first, delete the items, remove every connection, delete the collection, and, crucially, set up 301 redirects so you don’t break links or lose SEO. If there’s any chance you’ll need the content again, unpublish instead of deleting. And always test afterward. Handled this way, restructuring your CMS is a clean, low-risk change rather than a source of broken pages and lost rankings.

fieldData.meta-title: Is Webflow good for ecommerce? An honest 2026 answer | Nues
fieldData.meta-description: Is Webflow good for ecommerce? Yes, for the right kind of store. The honest limits, who it fits, who should look elsewhere, and the hybrid option.
fieldData.short-description: Webflow is genuinely good for ecommerce, but only for the right kind of store. The honest limits, who it fits best, who should look elsewhere, and the hybrid setup worth knowing about.
fieldData.tl-dr: Yes, Webflow is good for ecommerce, but only for the right store. It wins on design, speed, and SEO control, making it excellent for design-led brands, digital products, and small-to-mid catalogs. The limits are scale and complexity: a cap of 3,000 products and 50 variants each, plus a transaction fee on the entry plan. For large catalogs, complex inventory, dropshipping, or omnichannel, Shopify leads. A popular middle path is a hybrid: Webflow for the brand and content, Shopify for the checkout.
fieldData.content:
The honest answer: yes, but not for everyone

Since we’re a Webflow agency, you might expect the answer to be an enthusiastic “yes, of course.” It’s more honest than that. Webflow is genuinely good for ecommerce, but only for a specific kind of store, and being clear about which kind saves you from a frustrating rebuild later.

The short version: Webflow is an excellent ecommerce platform when design, speed, and content matter more than catalog scale and logistics automation. For a design-led brand with a focused product range, it’s often a better choice than a dedicated platform. For a high-volume store with thousands of products and complex inventory, it isn’t. The rest of this guide is about telling those two situations apart, so you can decide honestly.

What Webflow ecommerce does well

When Webflow fits, it has real, distinct advantages over template-based ecommerce platforms.

Design control

Webflow gives you full control over every part of the storefront, product grids, hover states, animations, page layouts, with no template constraints. Your store can feel like a genuinely branded experience rather than a checkout wrapper that looks like every other store on the same platform. For a brand that competes on identity, that’s a meaningful edge.

Speed and performance 

Because Webflow outputs clean code and doesn’t rely on heavy third-party app stacks, well-built stores load fast and score well on Core Web Vitals. In 2026, with buyers arriving already informed and impatient, that speed is a trust signal that compounds across the funnel.

SEO control 

You get full control over URL structures (Shopify locks you into /products/ and /collections/), fully editable robots.txt, custom meta titles and descriptions, and schema markup. For a brand that depends on organic traffic, this flexibility is a real advantage.

Content and commerce live together

 Webflow’s CMS means you can run a serious blog, editorial pages, and tutorials right alongside your products. For brands where content drives sales, and for B2B companies that use a product catalog to educate buyers and generate leads rather than sell directly, this combination is genuinely strong.

The limits you need to know

Being honest about the limits is the whole point, because they’re exactly what determines whether Webflow fits. None of these are secret, and all of them are easy to check against your own needs.

Catalog size and variants

Webflow caps out at 3,000 products and 50 variants per product. For comparison, Shopify supports effectively unlimited products and over 2,000 variants each. For a focused catalog, Webflow’s limits are fine. For a large or highly configurable product range, they’re often a dealbreaker.

Transaction fees

Webflow charges a 2% transaction fee on its entry Standard ecommerce plan, which drops to 0% on its higher plans. That’s worth factoring into the cost, especially at higher sales volumes.

Missing advanced features

Compared to a dedicated platform like Shopify, Webflow lacks native point-of-sale, deep discount and promotion logic, robust multi-currency, advanced shipping with real-time carrier rates, and abandoned cart recovery without add-ons. For simple stores these gaps don’t matter. For complex operations they add up.

Best for Design-led, content-driven, small-mid catalog Large catalogs, high-volume retail
Product limit Up to 3,000 Effectively unlimited
Variants per product Up to 50 Over 2,000
Design control Full, no template limits Template-based, less flexible
SEO control Among the best, full URL control Solid, but locked URL structure
Transaction fee 2% on entry plan, 0% on higher 0% with Shopify Payments
Native POS / omnichannel No Yes
Content + commerce Strong, built-in CMS Blog is more limited

Who Webflow ecommerce is right for

Webflow ecommerce is a strong choice, sometimes the best choice, for a few clear profiles.

Design-led DTC brands that compete on brand and want a storefront that looks like no one else’s. Digital products and course sellers with simple fulfillment and a focus on presentation. Small-to-mid catalogs, broadly under a few hundred products, where Webflow’s limits are comfortably above your needs. And B2B or content-driven commerce, where the catalog educates buyers, supports sales conversations, or generates leads, and where pricing can be gated and tied into a CRM rather than sold through a standard checkout.

The thread connecting these is that they value design, speed, conversion clarity, and content over catalog breadth and logistics automation. For them, Webflow isn’t a compromise. It’s an advantage.

Who should look elsewhere

It’s just as important to be clear about who Webflow ecommerce isn’t for, because forcing it to do the wrong job is how projects go wrong.

If you’re running a large catalog of thousands of products, complex inventory with intricate variants or warehousing, high-volume retail, dropshipping, or omnichannel operations spanning online and physical retail, a dedicated platform like Shopify or WooCommerce is the better fit. These platforms were built for commerce at scale, and they handle the logistics, automation, and product complexity that Webflow doesn’t. Choosing them over Webflow isn’t a knock on Webflow, it’s matching the tool to the job.

The hybrid option: Webflow + Shopify

There’s a third path that’s become increasingly popular in 2026, and it’s worth knowing about because it sidesteps the whole either/or choice.

In a Webflow + Shopify hybrid, you use Webflow for everything it’s best at, the homepage, editorial and brand pages, blog, and CMS, and connect to Shopify for the checkout, payments, inventory, and fulfillment. You get Webflow’s design and content strengths on the front end with Shopify’s commerce engine underneath. For brands that want a genuinely custom brand experience but also need serious commerce infrastructure, this combination delivers the best of both, and it’s a common setup for design-led brands that have outgrown Webflow’s native commerce but don’t want to give up its front-end control.

The honest verdict

So, is Webflow good for ecommerce? Yes, for the right store. If you’re a design-led brand, sell digital products, run a small-to-mid catalog, or use commerce to support a content or B2B strategy, Webflow is genuinely strong, often stronger than a template-based platform, thanks to its design, speed, and SEO control. If you run a large or complex store, Shopify or WooCommerce will serve you better, and there’s no shame in choosing the tool built for that job. And if you want both a custom brand experience and serious commerce infrastructure, the Webflow plus Shopify hybrid is worth a look. The real question was never “is Webflow good for ecommerce” in the abstract. It’s “is Webflow good for my store,” and now you have what you need to answer it.

fieldData.meta-description: A clear, step-by-step website redesign process: how to plan, structure, and run a redesign without losing SEO, time, or your mind.
fieldData.short-description: Most redesigns go wrong because they start with visuals instead of a plan. Here’s a clear, step-by-step process that protects your SEO and fixes what the old site actually got wrong.
fieldData.tl-dr: A redesign goes wrong when it starts with visuals instead of a plan. Done right, it's a sequence: define the problem first, audit what you have, plan structure and content before design, and protect your SEO with a redirect plan so you don't lose years of rankings. Then design, build, and test with real content, and treat launch as a starting point, not a finish line. It's a structured project, not a fresh coat of paint.
fieldData.content:
A redesign is a project, not a paint job

Most website redesigns start in the wrong place: with how the site looks. Someone decides the current site feels dated, a designer is briefed, and the project becomes about visuals. Months later there’s a prettier site that often performs no better, and sometimes worse, because the redesign never addressed why the old site wasn’t working.

A redesign done well is a structured process with a clear order, where each step builds on the last. Looks are part of it, but near the end, not the beginning. 

The seven steps

A redesign that protects what works and fixes what doesn’t, in order. Here’s the sequence that actually works.

Step 1: Define why you’re redesigning

Before anything else, get specific about the problem you’re solving. “It feels old” isn’t a reason. “Our bounce rate is high, the site doesn’t generate leads, and we can’t update it without a developer” is.

Write down the actual goals: more qualified leads, better mobile experience, easier content management, faster load times, a clearer message. These goals drive every later decision, and without them you have no way to judge whether the redesign succeeded. Define what success looks like in measurable terms now, so you can prove it later.

Step 2: Audit what you already have

You can’t improve a site you don’t understand. Before redesigning, take stock of the current one.

Look at the data: which pages get traffic, which convert, which rank in search, and which are dead weight. Your best-performing pages are assets to protect, not things to casually throw away. A redesign that accidentally removes or breaks a page that brought in steady leads is a step backward, however good it looks. This audit tells you what to keep, what to fix, and what to cut.

Step 3: Plan structure and content before design

This is the step most teams skip, and it’s the one that matters most. Structure comes before visuals.

Map the sitemap first: what pages exist, how they’re organized, how someone navigates from landing to conversion. Then sort out content, because design should present content, not the other way around. Designing beautiful pages and then trying to pour words in later is backwards, and it shows. Get your messaging and key content settled, at least in draft, before serious design begins.

Step 4: Protect your SEO (the step people forget)

This is where redesigns quietly destroy value. Search authority is earned slowly and lost fast, and a careless redesign can erase years of rankings overnight.

The essentials: map every old URL to its new equivalent and set up proper redirects so nothing breaks and no equity is lost. Keep the content and pages that rank well, preserve their structure where you can, and plan the migration so search engines follow you cleanly to the new site. If you take one thing from this guide, make it this. A redesign that loses your SEO is a failure no matter how good it looks. (For more on the technical side, our Webflow CMS and SEO coverage goes deeper.)

Step 5: Design, then build, with real content

Now, and only now, does design happen, and it happens with real content in hand, not lorem ipsum.

Design the key templates and pages around the structure and content you’ve already settled. Designing with real headlines, real copy, and real images produces a site that works in reality, not just in a mockup. Then build it properly: clean, fast, responsive, and easy for your team to manage afterward. A site that looks good but is slow or impossible to update has just recreated the original problem in a new skin.

Step 6: Test before you launch

Before going live, test everything. This is dull and it is also where launch disasters are prevented.

Check that pages work across browsers and devices, forms submit and reach where they should, links work, the site is fast, and every redirect resolves correctly. A staging environment lets you catch problems before users do. Walk the whole site as a visitor would, on a phone as well as a desktop, and fix what breaks before launch, not after.

Step 7: Launch carefully, then keep improving

Launch is a careful, monitored step, not a button you press and walk away from.

Go live with a plan: confirm redirects are working, check analytics is tracking, watch search performance in the days after, and be ready to fix anything that slipped through. Then remember the real point: a redesign is a starting line, not a finish line. The first version live is the beginning of improving based on real data, not the end of the project. The best sites are refined continuously, not redesigned in a panic every few years.

The short version

A good redesign follows an order: define why, audit what you have, plan structure and content, protect your SEO, then design, build, and test, and launch carefully. Skip the early steps and you get a prettier site that performs worse. Follow them and you get a site that actually fixes what the old one got wrong. The visual refresh is the easy part and the last part. The thinking that comes before it is what makes the difference.

fieldData.meta-title: Webflow templates: how to choose one | Nues
fieldData.meta-description: How to choose a Webflow template that fits: what to check in the CMS, design, and structure, and when to go custom instead.
fieldData.short-description: A good template saves you weeks of work, a bad one costs you a rebuild six months later. How to choose a Webflow template that actually fits, what to check before you buy, and when to go custom instead.
fieldData.tl-dr: A good Webflow template saves you time and money while a bad one costs you both in a rebuild later. The screenshot is the least important part. What matters underneath is does it fit your use case, is the CMS set up properly, is it fast on mobile, and are the classes clean enough to edit easily. Buy from the official Marketplace when you can, and know when your needs are specific enough that custom is the better call.
fieldData.content:
A template is a foundation, not a finished site

A Webflow template is a pre-built site you clone into your account and customize. The good ones give you a professional starting point and save weeks of work. The bad ones look great in the screenshot and then fight you the moment you try to make them yours.

The mistake most people make is choosing on looks alone. The design you see is the easy part to change, colors, fonts, images, copy. What’s hard to change is the structure underneath: how the CMS is set up, how clean the code is, how well it holds together on mobile. That’s what actually determines whether a template saves you time or costs you a rebuild.

What to check before you buy

Here’s what to look at, roughly in order of importance. Most template regret comes from skipping these. Run through them before you spend anything

Start with your use case, not the gallery

Before browsing a single template, get clear on what your site needs to do. A template built for one purpose rarely fits another well.

A SaaS or software site needs pricing tables, feature sections, space for product screenshots, and a CMS blog for content marketing. A portfolio needs to put visual work first, with strong project layouts and minimal distraction. An agency or service site needs service pages, case studies, and a clear contact path. An online store needs proper product, cart, and checkout structure.

Browsing by category from the start saves you from falling for a beautiful template that’s built for the wrong job. A stunning portfolio template will never become a good SaaS site without a full rebuild, and at that point the template saved you nothing.

Check the CMS setup first

This is the single most important technical thing, and it’s the one most people skip.

Webflow’s CMS is what lets your content scale: blog posts, case studies, team members, products, all managed cleanly. A template with a properly built CMS has collections already wired up with the right fields (author, category, date, slug for a blog, for example). A template without that, or with a fake “blog” that’s just static pages, will force a rebuild the moment you start publishing seriously.

Before choosing, check exactly what CMS collections the template includes and whether they match what you’ll publish. If you plan to run a content operation, and most businesses should, this matters more than any visual feature. A great-looking template with a weak CMS is a trap.

Test the live preview properly

Every template on the Webflow Marketplace has a live preview. Use it, and don’t just look at it on your desktop.

Open the preview on your phone. A large share of visitors will see your site on mobile first, and many desktop-pretty templates fall apart on small screens. Check that layouts hold, text stays readable, and nothing overflows. Then check speed, run the live preview through a tool like Google’s PageSpeed Insights and aim for a strong score. A slow template frustrates visitors and hurts your search rankings, and heavy templates loaded with uncompressed images and excessive animation are slow from day one.

Five minutes in the live preview, on a phone and through a speed test, tells you more than any screenshot.

Look at the structure, not just the style

This one’s less obvious but it’s what separates a template you can actually edit from one you’ll struggle with.

A well-built template uses clean, logically named CSS classes and Webflow’s global styles and variables, so you can change colors, fonts, and spacing across the whole site in a few clicks. A badly built one has messy, inconsistent classes that make every edit a guessing game. You can’t always see this from the preview, but template descriptions, reviews, and the designer’s reputation give you signals. Templates that mention clean class naming, global variables, and Webflow best practices are usually safer.

The test is simple: a good template should make it easy to change anything. If editing feels like fighting the build, the template was made to look good in a screenshot, not to be used.

Buy from the official Marketplace when you can

You can get Webflow templates from the official Webflow Marketplace or from third-party designers and template clubs. Both can be good, but they carry different risk.

The official Marketplace vets templates for quality and code standards, every template has a live preview, and support is more reliable. Third-party templates sometimes offer more unique designs or specialized focuses, but you need to verify they’re actively maintained and that the seller provides support before buying. Template subscriptions can be cost-effective if you’re launching several sites, but only if the quality holds up.

As a default, especially if you’re not confident judging a build yourself, start with the official Marketplace. The quality floor is higher and you’re less likely to end up with something abandoned.

A note on price: template prices change often, and they range from free to a few hundred dollars. Any number you see in a roundup article (including this one) is a snapshot, so check the current price on the Marketplace before buying. As a rough guide, paid templates generally offer better design quality and more complete page sets than free ones, but Webflow’s own free templates (like its SaaS and Startup starters) are technically solid for an MVP.

Know when a template isn’t the answer

Templates are the right call for a lot of situations. But they’re not always, and it’s worth being honest about when custom is the better investment.

A template works well when your needs are fairly standard, you want to launch fast, and budget is tight. It struggles when you need something specific, a unique brand expression, custom functionality, a complex content structure, or a design that genuinely sets you apart. Forcing a template to do something it wasn’t built for often costs more in workarounds than custom would have cost up front, and you still end up with a compromise.

The honest rule: if your site is fairly standard and speed matters most, a good template is smart. If your site is core to how your business competes, and the design and structure need to be exactly right, custom is usually the better long-term investment. Plenty of companies start on a template and move to custom once they’ve outgrown it, and that’s a perfectly sensible path.

The short version

Choosing a Webflow template comes down to looking past the screenshot. Match it to your use case, check the CMS setup, test the live preview on mobile and for speed, and favor clean structure and the official Marketplace. And know the limits: a template is a fast, affordable foundation, but when your site needs to be genuinely distinctive or do something specific, custom is what gets you there. Choose with that in mind and a template can save you real time. Choose on looks alone and you’ll be rebuilding by next quarter.

In 2026 that line has blurred, mostly because of Wix Studio, the professional version of Wix aimed at agencies and advanced users. fieldData.content:
The Webflow vs Wix comparison changed in 2026

For years, comparing Webflow and Wix was simple. Wix was the easy drag-and-drop builder for beginners and small businesses. Webflow was the professional tool for designers and agencies who wanted full control. If that’s how you’ve always thought about these two, you weren’t wrong. That’s exactly how both platforms positioned themselves for a long time.

But in 2026, those labels have started to break down, and an honest comparison has to acknowledge why. Wix has been working hard to move beyond its beginner-builder reputation, especially with Wix Studio, its push toward agencies and larger organizations. At the same time, Webflow has been moving deeper into the business and team space with stronger collaboration, AI tools, and features like localization. The two are no longer at opposite ends of a simple line.

So this isn’t a “pro tool versus easy tool” comparison anymore. It’s a more interesting question: now that Wix has a serious professional offering, where does Webflow still lead, and where does Wix genuinely win? This guide answers that honestly, from the perspective of a Webflow agency that pays attention to what the competition is actually doing well.

Standard Wix vs Wix Studio: which are we comparing?

Before comparing anything, there’s a distinction that most Wix versus Webflow articles skip, and skipping it makes the whole comparison misleading. There are two versions of Wix, and they’re aimed at very different people.

Standard Wix is the original drag-and-drop builder. It’s designed for beginners, small business owners, and anyone who wants to get a good-looking site online fast without thinking about technical details. You drag elements onto the page, the AI can generate a layout for you, and you’re live in hours. This is the Wix most people picture.

Wix Studio is the professional version of the Wix ecosystem, built for agencies, freelancers, and advanced users. It adds a true responsive grid system, reusable components, and more scalable workflows, which are the things standard Wix historically lacked. Wix Studio is Wix’s real answer to Webflow, and it closes a lot of the gap that older comparison articles still describe.

This matters for the rest of the guide. When we say Webflow leads on design control, that gap is large against standard Wix and much smaller against Wix Studio. So throughout this comparison, the honest framing is: standard Wix and Webflow are aimed at different users, while Wix Studio and Webflow are genuine competitors. We’ll be clear about which one we mean where it matters.

Area Standard Wix Wix Studio Webflow
Best for Beginners, small business Agencies, pro projects Growing B2B, marketing
Design control Drag-and-drop, limited Responsive grid, strong Pixel-level, top end
Learning curve Easiest Moderate Steepest
CMS Basic More capable Built for scale
SEO control Improved, AI tools Improved Full technical control
Launch speed Fastest Fast Slower, more setup
All-in-one Fully bundled Bundled More modular
Scales as it grows Limited Better Built to scale
Entry pricing From ~$17/mo From ~$17/mo From ~$14/mo

When each one fits

Each platform suits a different kind of team and project. Here’s where each one is the better call.

When Wix is the right choice

Wix, in both forms, genuinely wins in a set of situations, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. Here’s where it’s the smarter pick.

If you’re a beginner or a small business owner who wants a professional site online fast, standard Wix is hard to beat. The drag-and-drop editor is genuinely intuitive, the AI site generator can produce a starting layout from a few questions, and you can go from nothing to live in hours without any technical knowledge. For a local business, a personal brand, or anyone who values speed and simplicity over control, Wix delivers exactly that.

If you want everything built in with no assembly, Wix’s all-in-one approach is a real strength. Hosting, security, e-commerce, booking, email marketing, and business tools come bundled. You don’t think about plugins or integrations. For a business owner who wants to run their business rather than their website, that bundling is genuinely useful.

If you need to launch microsites or campaign pages fast, Wix is well suited to it. Even large companies like Walmart, Nikon, and Renault Group use Wix, not for their main sites, but for microsites and subsidiary pages that need to go live quickly. That’s a real and sensible use case, and Wix handles it well.

If you’re an agency or freelancer who wants a faster, simpler workflow than Webflow for certain projects, Wix Studio is now a credible option. Its responsive grid and reusable components make it capable for professional work, and for some teams the gentler learning curve is worth the trade in control. It doesn’t match Webflow in every advanced area, but it’s a real tool, not a toy.

The pattern is that Wix wins when speed, simplicity, and all-in-one convenience matter most, whether that’s a beginner building their first site or an agency moving fast on a straightforward project. For those cases, Wix is the right call, not a compromise.

When Webflow is the better choice

Webflow becomes the better platform when a site needs to do serious, scalable work, especially for content-driven and marketing-led businesses. Here’s where it still leads, including against Wix Studio.

The clearest reason is design control at the top end. Webflow gives pixel-level command over layout, animation, and responsive behavior, and generates clean, professional code underneath. Wix Studio has closed part of this gap with its responsive grid, but for the most demanding design work, building a precise brand system, complex interactions, fully custom layouts, Webflow still offers more control and cleaner output. For a company whose site is a core brand asset, that ceiling matters.

The second reason is content at scale. Webflow’s CMS handles complex, interrelated content, relational references, dynamic filtering, and template pages that generate from CMS data. For a serious blog, a growing case study library, a resource center, or programmatic landing pages, Webflow’s CMS is built for that scale in a way Wix’s is not. Wix can manage content, but as it grows into hundreds of structured items, Webflow’s CMS is the stronger engine.

The third reason is marketing autonomy and stability at scale. Webflow lets a marketing team build, test, and ship without a developer, and sites tend to stay stable and fast as they grow. Wix performance depends heavily on how the builder is used; adding many third-party apps or heavy elements can slow a site down. For a growing site that needs to stay fast and let marketing move quickly, Webflow tends to be more predictable over time.

The fourth reason is SEO control. Webflow gives complete control over technical SEO, with editable meta titles, descriptions, and alt text at both static and CMS levels, plus clean code that search engines and AI tools read easily. Wix has improved its SEO tools and added AI features, but for a serious organic strategy, Webflow’s level of control is still ahead.

The honest framing is that Webflow is the better choice when control, content scale, marketing speed, and long-term SEO matter more than launch speed and simplicity. That’s usually a growing, content-driven business with a marketing team, which is a different situation from the small business or fast microsite that Wix serves so well.

The details that matter

Where the two genuinely differ, feature by feature.

Design and customization

This is where the standard Wix versus Wix Studio distinction matters most, so it’s worth being specific.

Against standard Wix, Webflow’s design advantage is large. Standard Wix uses a simpler drag-and-drop model that’s easy to learn but limits fine control, especially over responsive behavior across devices. Webflow gives granular control over every element and breakpoint, with clean code underneath. For any design-led project, Webflow is clearly ahead of standard Wix.

Against Wix Studio, the gap narrows. Wix Studio added a true responsive grid system, reusable components, and more professional workflows, which address the biggest historical complaints. For many professional projects, Wix Studio is now genuinely capable. Webflow still leads at the top end, with more precise control and cleaner output for the most demanding work, but the difference is smaller than older articles suggest, and for some projects Wix Studio’s faster workflow is a fair trade.

The honest summary on design: if you’re comparing Webflow to standard Wix, Webflow wins on control comfortably. If you’re comparing Webflow to Wix Studio, both are capable professional tools, and the choice comes down to how much top-end control you need versus how fast you want to move. Either way, Webflow gives you the most design ceiling, and Wix gives you the faster path to a polished result.

CMS and content scaling

If content is central to your strategy, the platforms diverge.

Wix handles content well for smaller, simpler needs. A blog, a portfolio, a modest collection of items, all of these work cleanly, and Wix Studio adds more capability for professional content work. For a business that publishes occasionally or runs a contained content operation, Wix is perfectly capable.

Webflow’s CMS is built for scale and complexity. It supports many interrelated content types, relational references between them, dynamic filtering and sorting, and templates that generate pages automatically from CMS content. For a marketing operation publishing case studies, comparison pages, integration pages, and a regular blog, all with custom structures, Webflow’s CMS does work that a simpler system isn’t designed for. As content grows from dozens of items into the hundreds, that depth becomes the difference between scaling smoothly and fighting the platform.

This matters most for content-driven and B2B companies. If publishing structured content over time is central to your growth, the CMS is the engine of your marketing, and Webflow gives that engine more room to run.

SEO and pricing

Two practical factors that often decide the choice.

On SEO, Webflow leads. It gives complete control over technical SEO, editable meta titles, descriptions, and alt text at both static and CMS levels, plus clean, semantic code that’s easy for search engines and AI search tools to read. Wix has genuinely improved its SEO tools and added AI-assisted features, and for a straightforward site it’s adequate. But for a serious organic strategy where technical control matters, Webflow is still ahead.

On pricing, the two are close at the entry level. Webflow’s paid plans start at around $14 a month and Wix’s at around $17, so there’s little between them to start. Both also offer free tiers to test, though Wix’s free plan is more functional for a live site while Webflow’s free tier is mainly for staging. As always, both platforms adjust pricing regularly, so check the current plans on their sites. The more meaningful cost difference is the same as with any Webflow comparison: serious Webflow work often involves an agency or developer, so the total investment reflects a different class of site, not just a different subscription.

A decision framework

Here’s the simplest way to decide, based on everything above.

Choose Wix if most of these are true:

  • You’re a beginner or small business that wants a professional site online fast
  • You want everything bundled with no technical setup
  • You’re launching microsites or campaign pages that need to go live quickly
  • You value speed and simplicity over fine-grained control
  • You’re an agency wanting a faster, simpler workflow for a straightforward project (Wix Studio)

Choose Webflow if most of these are true:

  • You’re a growing, content-driven company, often B2B
  • Your website is a core brand asset that needs precise design control
  • You’re publishing content at scale, with a blog, case studies, or a resource library
  • Your marketing team needs to move fast and the site needs to stay fast as it grows
  • Serious technical SEO is a real growth channel
  • You need the highest design ceiling, even compared to Wix Studio

The honest summary. Wix is excellent at what it’s for: getting a site live fast, with everything included, and with Wix Studio it’s now a credible professional tool too. For beginners, small businesses, fast microsites, and some agency projects, it’s a smart choice. Webflow is the better pick when control, content scale, marketing speed, and long-term SEO matter more than launch speed, which usually means a growing, content-driven business with a marketing team. The honest takeaway isn’t that one platform beats the other. It’s that the line between them has blurred, so the right choice depends more than ever on what your specific site needs to do, now and as it grows.

The real difference between Webflow and Squarespace

Most comparisons frame this as a fight, with a winner at the end. That’s the wrong way to look at it. Webflow and Squarespace are built on different philosophies, for different kinds of users, and the better question isn’t which is better in the abstract. It’s which fits the site you’re trying to build.

Squarespace is built around guided simplicity. You pick a beautiful template, fill it with your content, and you have a polished, professional site live in an afternoon. Everything is included: hosting, a domain, e-commerce, email marketing, analytics, all in one subscription. The trade-off you accept is control. You work within the template’s structure, and when you want something it wasn’t designed to do, you hit a wall.

Webflow is built around control. It gives you near-code-level command over design, a CMS that scales to complex content, and the freedom to build almost anything without writing code yourself. The trade-off is that this power takes time to learn, and getting the most out of it usually means working with an experienced developer or agency. Webflow rewards the investment with a site that can grow in any direction, but it asks for that investment up front.

That’s the real difference. Squarespace optimizes for getting live fast with less control. Webflow optimizes for control and scale at the cost of simplicity. Neither is wrong. They’re built for different stages and different needs, and the rest of this guide is about figuring out which one is yours.

Area Squarespace Webflow
Best for Small business, solo, creatives Growing B2B, marketing teams
Design control Template-based, curated Pixel-level, near-code
Learning curve Gentle, DIY-friendly Steep, 40-60 hours
CMS Good for basic content Built for content at scale
E-commerce Strong, on every plan Capable, higher tiers
Marketing autonomy Limited by template Ship and test freely
All-in-one Yes, fully bundled More modular
Needs a developer No, built for DIY Often an agency or dev
Entry pricing From around $16/mo From around $15/mo
Room to grow Hits a ceiling eventually Scales in any direction

When each one fits

One gets you online fast, the other grows with you. Which is right depends on your needs and where you’re headed.

When Squarespace is the right choice

It would be dishonest to treat Squarespace as the lesser option. For a large set of businesses, it’s the smarter pick, and here’s where it genuinely wins.

If you’re a small business, a solo founder, or a creative professional who needs a professional site quickly and cheaply, Squarespace is hard to beat. The templates are genuinely beautiful, the editor is intuitive, and you can go from nothing to a live, polished site in a day without hiring anyone. For a restaurant, a photographer, a consultant, or a local service business, that speed and simplicity is exactly what’s needed.

If you want everything in one place with no assembly required, Squarespace’s all-in-one approach is a real advantage. Hosting, domain, e-commerce, email marketing, scheduling, and analytics come bundled. You don’t think about plugins, integrations, or technical setup. For a business owner who wants to run their business, not their website, that bundling removes a genuine burden.

If you want to sell simply, Squarespace’s e-commerce is strong out of the box. Every plan includes the ability to take payments, and the platform handles product listings, shipping, in-person POS, and multi-channel selling without add-ons. For a small online store or a business adding a shop to its site, Squarespace’s commerce is more accessible than Webflow’s, especially on lower-priced plans.

If you don’t have a developer and don’t want one, Squarespace is designed for exactly that. It’s built for DIY use, and most people can run their own Squarespace site indefinitely without technical help. That self-sufficiency is part of its appeal, and for many businesses it’s the deciding factor.

The pattern across these cases is that Squarespace wins when simplicity, speed, and self-sufficiency matter more than control and scale. For a lot of businesses, that’s the right trade, and choosing Squarespace is the smart call, not a compromise.

When Webflow is the better choice

Webflow becomes the better platform when your needs outgrow what guided simplicity can offer. For growing B2B companies, marketing teams, and content-driven businesses, that point usually arrives sooner than expected.

The clearest reason is design control. Webflow gives pixel-level command over layout, animation, and responsive behavior, which means your site can match your brand exactly rather than approximating it within a template. For a company whose website is a core part of how it’s perceived, the difference between “looks like our brand” and “looks like a Squarespace template” is real, and it compounds as the brand matures.

The second reason is content at scale. Webflow’s CMS handles complex, interrelated content in a way Squarespace’s simpler system can’t. If you’re running a serious blog, a growing case study library, a resource center, or programmatic landing pages, Webflow’s CMS is built for that scale. Squarespace handles a basic blog fine, but it wasn’t designed for content operations that grow into the hundreds of items with custom structures.

The third reason is marketing autonomy. This is where Webflow quietly pulls ahead for B2B teams. A marketing team can build landing pages, run tests, and ship changes without waiting on engineering, and without being boxed in by a template. For a team whose job is to keep the site moving at the speed of the business, that freedom is the whole point, and it’s something a template-based platform structurally can’t match.

The fourth reason is room to grow. A Webflow site doesn’t hit a ceiling the way a template-based site eventually does. Whatever you need next, a custom integration, a complex interaction, a new content type, a redesign without starting over, Webflow can accommodate it. For a business that expects its website needs to get more demanding over time, that headroom matters.

The honest framing is that Webflow is the better choice when control, scale, and marketing speed start to matter more than simplicity. That’s usually a growing company with a marketing team and a website that has real work to do, which is a different situation from the small business Squarespace serves so well.

Details that matter

Where the two genuinely differ, feature by feature.

Design and customization

This is the starkest difference between the two, and it’s worth being specific about.

Webflow offers near-complete design freedom. You control layout, spacing, typography, animation, and responsive behavior down to the pixel, and the platform generates clean, professional code underneath. Designers can replicate a brand system exactly, build custom interactions, and create something genuinely distinctive. The catch is the learning curve. Most people need somewhere in the range of 40 to 60 hours to become proficient with Webflow’s interface and concepts like classes and flexbox, which is why serious Webflow work is often done by an agency or experienced developer.

Squarespace takes the opposite approach. It offers a curated set of around 300 professionally designed templates, and you customize within their structure. You can adjust colors, fonts, images, and content easily, but you’re working inside the template’s design decisions rather than making your own from scratch. For most users this is a feature, not a limitation, because the templates are well-made and the constraints keep the result looking polished. The limit shows up when you want something the template wasn’t built for, where advanced customization often requires workarounds or custom code.

The simple way to think about it: Squarespace gives you a beautiful set of options to choose from, and Webflow gives you a blank canvas and the tools to build anything. One values guardrails, the other values freedom. Which is right depends on whether your priority is a polished result fast, or a custom result that’s exactly yours.

CMS and content scaling

If content is central to your strategy, the two platforms diverge quickly.

Squarespace’s CMS handles the basics well. A blog, a portfolio, a simple collection of items, all of these work cleanly and are easy to manage. For a business that publishes occasionally and doesn’t need complex content structures, it’s perfectly capable.

Webflow’s CMS is built for scale and complexity. It supports many interrelated content types, relational references between them, dynamic filtering and sorting, and template pages that generate automatically from CMS content. For a marketing operation publishing case studies, comparison pages, integration pages, and a regular blog, all with custom structures, Webflow’s CMS does work that Squarespace’s simpler system isn’t designed for. As content grows from dozens of items to hundreds, that difference becomes the difference between a system that scales and one you fight against.

This matters most for B2B and content-driven companies. If your growth depends on publishing a lot of structured content over time, the CMS is not a minor detail, it’s the engine of your marketing. Webflow gives that engine far more room to run.

E-commerce

Here the comparison flips from the rest of the guide, and it’s worth being honest about.

For simple, accessible e-commerce, Squarespace is the stronger choice. Every Squarespace plan includes the ability to take payments, and the platform bundles product management, shipping, in-person POS, and multi-channel selling without extra tools. For a small store, a business adding a shop, or anyone who wants to start selling quickly without technical setup, Squarespace’s commerce is more approachable, especially on its lower-priced plans where Webflow doesn’t include payment processing at all.

Webflow’s e-commerce is capable but positioned differently. It gives you full design control over the shopping experience and works well for limited-to-medium catalogs, but it shows up on higher-tier plans and generally suits businesses that want a custom storefront over a quick one. For a content-driven B2B company that sells a few things, it’s fine. For a business whose primary model is e-commerce, especially a smaller one, Squarespace’s all-in-one commerce is usually the more practical pick.

The honest takeaway: if selling is central to your business and you want it simple, Squarespace has the edge here. If e-commerce is secondary to a content or marketing site and you want it to match a custom design, Webflow works well. This is one area where Squarespace genuinely leads for a lot of use cases.

Pricing and total cost

On paper, the two are priced similarly. Webflow’s paid site plans start around $15 a month and Squarespace’s start around $16, so at the entry level there’s little between them. Both also offer a free trial period to test before committing, and both regularly adjust their pricing, so it’s worth checking the current plans on their sites.

The real cost picture has some nuance, though. Webflow adds a transaction fee on its lower e-commerce tiers, and because Webflow’s power often means working with an agency or developer, the true cost of a Webflow project usually includes that build investment. Squarespace’s cost is more self-contained, since most people build and run it themselves, so the subscription is closer to the full cost.

The honest way to read pricing is not which subscription is cheaper, because they’re close, but what the total investment looks like for your situation. A solo business owner building their own Squarespace site has a low, predictable cost. A growing company building a custom Webflow site with an agency is making a larger investment, but it’s buying a different class of website. Comparing only the monthly subscription misses most of the real picture.

A decision framework

Here’s the simplest way to decide, based on everything above.

Choose Squarespace if most of these are true:

  • You’re a small business, solo founder, or creative professional
  • You want a polished, professional site live quickly and cheaply
  • You want everything bundled with no technical setup
  • You’re running a simple online store and want commerce that works out of the box
  • You don’t have a developer and don’t want one
  • Simplicity matters more to you than total control

Choose Webflow if most of these are true:

  • You’re a growing company with a marketing team
  • Your website is central to how your brand is perceived and needs to be exactly right
  • You’re publishing content at scale, with a blog, case studies, or a resource library
  • Your marketing team needs to move fast without being boxed in by a template
  • You expect your website needs to get more demanding over time
  • You have, or are willing to work with, an experienced developer or agency

The honest summary. Squarespace is excellent at what it’s for: getting a polished, all-in-one site live fast, with no technical overhead. For a huge number of businesses, that’s exactly right, and Webflow would be overkill. Webflow is for when you outgrow that, when control, content scale, and marketing speed start to matter more than simplicity. Many successful businesses start on Squarespace and move to Webflow when they hit its limits, and that’s a perfectly sensible path. The question isn’t which platform is better. It’s which one matches where your business is now, and where it’s going next.
